Baby & Child

Tooth decay in children: causes, treatment and prevention

Updated: October 7, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

A cavity in a baby tooth deserves attention even though that tooth will eventually fall out. Decay can affect eating, comfort and the teeth that follow. Knowing the early signs and the range of treatment options can help you seek care before the problem becomes painful or more complicated.

Why baby teeth need treatment too

Decay can affect both baby and permanent teeth. Baby teeth help a child chew and speak and hold space for the teeth that follow. A painful or infected tooth should not be left untreated simply because it will eventually fall out. Even a child aged one or two may need dental treatment.

The word decay covers different stages. Early mineral loss in enamel may be stopped or reversed with appropriate care. Once a hole has formed, that lost tooth structure does not grow back through brushing alone. A dentist can explain whether the aim is to repair a cavity, stop its progression or protect an area before a hole develops.

How plaque, food and other factors contribute

Plaque is the sticky film that builds up on teeth. Bacteria in it use sugars and starches from food and drink and produce acids. Repeated acid exposure removes minerals from the tooth surface. Fluoride and saliva help protect teeth, but frequent exposure can overwhelm that protection.

Sweets, cake, ice cream and sugary drinks are familiar examples, but crackers, chips and other starchy snacks can also contribute. How often a child snacks or sips matters as well as the amount. Foods marketed as natural or healthy are not automatically harmless to teeth.

Brushing and cleaning between teeth reduce plaque, but cavities are not proof that a family has been careless. Saliva, fluoride exposure, enamel development, medicines, feeding patterns, access to care and difficulties tolerating brushing can affect risk. Some enamel conditions make teeth more vulnerable; a parent cannot diagnose genetic soft teeth just by looking at a cavity.

Signs to notice, even without pain

New chalky-white spots, brown or dark areas, a visible hole or sensitivity to cold or sweet foods can indicate a problem. Young children may cry during meals, become unusually irritable, avoid food or chew on one side. A colour change can have another explanation too, so arrange a dental examination rather than diagnosing it from a photograph.

Decay may not hurt at first. Regular visits can identify changes before a child can describe them. Book the first visit when teeth appear and by the first birthday; then follow the interval recommended for the child’s risk. Six months is common, but it is not the right fixed interval for every child.

Swelling, fever, persistent pain or a child becoming very unwell needs urgent dental assessment. Significant mouth swelling, difficulty breathing, speaking or swallowing, trouble opening the mouth, or swelling around an eye requires emergency care. Do not wait for the next routine check-up or assume unusual lethargy is only a tooth problem.

What fillings and other early treatments can do

The dentist assesses how deep the decay is, which tooth is involved and whether the child has pain or infection. Early changes may be managed with fluoride and changes to daily care. Sealants can protect suitable grooves in back teeth. A formed cavity may need restoration, but drilling and filling is not the only possible approach in every situation.

A filling replaces damaged tooth structure and helps preserve the tooth. Materials may include tooth-coloured restorations or another appropriate material, depending on the tooth, the child’s circumstances and local guidance. The dentist should explain what will be used and why. Restorations can be placed in baby as well as permanent teeth.

Silver diamine fluoride is another option for selected decay. It can help arrest a lesion but permanently blackens the decayed area, so families need to understand the appearance and follow-up before agreeing. It is different from routine fluoride varnish and does not restore a tooth’s original shape.

When a crown, pulp treatment or extraction is considered

A badly damaged baby tooth may need a crown to cover and protect it. Stainless-steel crowns are a familiar silver-coloured option, although the choice depends on the tooth and clinical plan. Decay close to or involving the tooth’s pulp may require additional treatment rather than a small filling.

If a tooth cannot be kept safely, removal may be needed. A dentist then considers whether a space maintainer would help preserve room for the permanent tooth. This is an individual decision based on the tooth lost and the stage of development, not an automatic requirement after every extraction.

Ask which teeth need prompt care, which can be monitored and what happens if treatment is delayed. A dental infection may need drainage, treatment inside the tooth or extraction. Antibiotics, when indicated, do not by themselves repair the source of the problem.

Helping a child feel comfortable during treatment

Explanation, familiarisation, breaks and a manageable appointment length can help. Local anaesthetic numbs the treatment area. Nitrous oxide, often called laughing gas, can reduce anxiety while a child usually remains awake; it does not automatically replace local numbing for painful treatment.

Some children may need medicine for sedation. Oral medicine is one possible route, but the drug, depth of sedation and monitoring matter more than calling it something to relax the child. Do not give sedatives at home unless the treating team has provided a specific supervised plan.

When several teeth need care, staged visits may suit some children. Others may need a different approach to avoid repeated distress or delaying urgent treatment. Ask the team to explain the sequence, how pain will be controlled and what alternatives are available.

What general anaesthesia means

General anaesthesia makes the child unconscious for treatment and requires a trained anaesthesia team and appropriate monitoring. It differs from lighter sedation or nitrous oxide. Extensive disease, very young age, disability or inability to complete necessary treatment safely may influence the recommendation; difficulty sitting still alone is not a complete risk-benefit assessment.

Ask who will provide and monitor the anaesthesia, where care will take place, which teeth will be treated and how recovery will be managed. Discuss medical conditions, medicines and previous reactions. Follow the team’s fasting and medicine instructions exactly, and report a new illness before the procedure.

The decision should weigh the risks and benefits of treatment and its alternatives, including the consequences of untreated pain or infection. A plan for preventing new decay is still needed after a successful procedure.

A brushing routine that grows with the child

Before teeth appear, gently wiping the gums with a clean soft damp cloth can help establish a mouth-care routine. Once the first tooth emerges, begin brushing with fluoride toothpaste. A cloth does not replace brushing teeth.

Brush twice daily, including last thing before bed, aiming for about two minutes as the routine develops. Under age three use a tiny smear of toothpaste, about the size of a grain of rice; from three to six use a pea-sized amount. Ask the dental team about the fluoride strength appropriate to local guidance and your child’s risk.

An adult should do or closely help with young children’s brushing. Many still need supervision beyond age six or seven; skill and thoroughness matter more than a birthday. Encourage spitting without immediately rinsing, and keep the tube out of reach so toothpaste is not eaten.

Help clean between touching teeth daily using the method your dentist demonstrates. Flossing can be difficult for small hands. A predictable routine, a soft age-appropriate brush and small choices can make cooperation easier. Pain, sensory distress or disability may require adaptations from the dental team rather than more pressure on the child.

Choose snacks and drinks with teeth and safety in mind

Reduce repeated sugary drinks and grazing between meals. Do not leave a baby in bed with a bottle or let milk or juice become an all-night bottle comforter. Discuss normal infant feeding needs and tooth care together with the dental team; feeding advice should account for the baby’s age and needs.

Whole fruit, including berries, plain yoghurt, suitable pieces of cheese, soft banana and prepared vegetables can be part of a varied diet. Unsweetened applesauce or other fruit purées may also fit meals, but no snack label guarantees cavity protection. The glycaemic index is not a reliable way to rank foods for tooth safety.

Dried fruit, trail mix and granola can contain concentrated or added sugars and may stick to teeth; they are not unlimited substitutes for sweets. Avoid hard frozen banana chunks, whole nuts, hard raw carrot pieces and other choking hazards for young children. Adapt texture and size to the child’s abilities, and supervise eating while the child is seated.

Keep follow-up appointments after a filling, crown or other treatment. Repairing one tooth does not remove the causes of decay. Supported cleaning, fluoride, sensible meal and snack routines and regular review can reduce future risk without promising that a child will never have another cavity.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Early mineral loss may be reversible; a formed cavity needs an individual dental plan. Treatment choices depend on the tooth, depth of disease and child.

Fluoride toothpaste, adult-supported cleaning and fewer repeated sugar exposures help prevention. Check-up intervals, sedation and space maintenance are individual decisions.

How BeMama can help

Keep questions about pain, brushing difficulties, planned treatments and follow-up together for your child’s dental visit. BeMama cannot diagnose a cavity or choose a sedation plan.

When to seek help

Seek urgent dental care for swelling, fever or suspected infection. Airway or swallowing difficulty, extensive mouth swelling or eye involvement requires emergency care.

Evidence notes updated: October 7, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Baby teeth support eating, speech and space for permanent teeth.
  • Decay may develop before pain appears.
  • Treatment can include prevention, arresting decay, restoration or extraction, depending on the case.
  • Sedation and general anaesthesia need separate explanations and monitoring plans.
  • Daily prevention and dental follow-up remain important after treatment.

Frequently asked questions

Should we wait for a decayed baby tooth to fall out?

No. Pain, infection and early tooth loss can affect a child before the normal replacement time. Ask a dentist what the tooth needs.

Can my child have decay without pain?

Yes. A new spot or visible defect may appear before pain. Regular examinations can find problems a child cannot describe.

Does every white spot mean a cavity?

No. White areas can have several causes, and early mineral loss may not yet be a hole. A dental assessment is needed.

Does every cavity need drilling?

Not always. Some lesions can be managed with an arresting treatment or another approach, while others need a filling or crown. The dentist should explain the choice.

Why can silver diamine fluoride turn a tooth black?

It darkens the decayed tissue it treats. This appearance change should be explained before treatment; it is not the same as a routine fluoride varnish.

Is a space maintainer always needed after an extraction?

No. The dentist considers the tooth lost, the child’s development and the available space before recommending one.

Is laughing gas the same as general anaesthesia?

No. With nitrous oxide a child usually remains awake. General anaesthesia involves unconsciousness and a different staffing and monitoring plan.

Can a six-year-old brush alone?

Some children still need considerable help at that age and beyond. Supervise until they can clean all surfaces effectively, and keep checking the routine.

Are dried fruit and granola automatically better for teeth?

No. Sugar concentration, stickiness and frequency matter, even without added sugar. Consider age-safe textures and balanced meals rather than a tooth-safe label.

Do fillings prevent all future cavities?

No. They treat existing damage. Fluoride, supported cleaning, food routines and follow-up are still needed to reduce new decay.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
